report:
**Conclusion: probably no.** Coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) has not been shown to produce a reliable, clinically meaningful improvement in Parkinson’s movement symptoms (such as slowness, rigidity, tremor, or overall motor-scale scores).

**Why this is the best-supported answer**

* There was a plausible rationale: CoQ10 supports mitochondrial energy function and acts as an antioxidant; laboratory models and an earlier phase-II trial suggested possible benefit. The early study of 28 people reported a *mild* symptomatic improvement versus placebo, so the question was reasonable to test. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12697283/
* But the more decisive evidence was negative. The Parkinson Study Group’s randomized high-dose trial in early Parkinson’s tested 1,200 or 2,400 mg/day versus placebo. It found CoQ10 safe and generally well tolerated, **but no evidence of clinical benefit**; it was stopped early after meeting a prespecified futility criterion. Its aim was slowing disease progression, rather than short-term symptom relief, but its clinical outcome measures include the relevant motor/disability progression. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24664227/?dopt=Abstract
* A meta-analysis of randomized trials likewise concluded CoQ10 was no better than placebo for motor outcomes, while appearing tolerable. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27830343/
* A later systematic review notes that some small studies reported mild motor-scale improvements, but the overall evidence—including multiple meta-analyses—does not establish efficacy. https://www.mdpi.com/2075-4426/12/6/975

Thus, your answer is supported: CoQ10 should not be expected to improve Parkinson’s movement disorder symptoms or slow their progression. “No proven benefit” is more accurate than proof that no individual could ever feel better. Discuss supplements with the treating clinician, particularly because they can add cost, side effects, and medication-management complexity.
